#!/usr/bin/env bash
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 Volkert de Buisonjé <volkertb@users.noreply.github.com>
# SPDX-FileContributor: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
#
# Regenerates seccomp.json: Docker's default seccomp profile, plus the syscalls bubblewrap
# needs to build an unprivileged user-namespace sandbox (what Codex's Linux sandbox uses).
# The default profile allows these only with CAP_SYS_ADMIN, which the container does not
# have. Run this to pick up upstream changes to the default profile; the output is committed.
#
# Usage: .devcontainer/make-seccomp.sh   (needs curl and jq)
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")"
src=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/profiles/main/seccomp/default.json
allow='["unshare","clone","mount","umount2","pivot_root","setns"]'

curl -fsSL "$src" | jq --argjson allow "$allow" '
  # Drop the syscalls from every existing rule (the CAP_SYS_ADMIN-gated ones and the
  # flag-masked clone rules), remove rules left empty, then allow them unconditionally.
  .syscalls |= map(.names -= $allow | select(.names | length > 0))
  | .syscalls += [{
      names: $allow,
      action: "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW",
      comment: "Unprivileged user namespaces for bubblewrap (Codex sandbox). Added by make-seccomp.sh."
    }]
' > seccomp.json

echo "Wrote $(pwd)/seccomp.json from $src"

A Responses-shaped object back means the integration surface is good; then just run `codex`.
For a one-off test against a different endpoint without editing the config,
`CODEX_OSS_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9931/v1` overrides Codex's built-in OSS provider.

### Codex's Linux sandbox

Codex runs commands inside a bubblewrap sandbox, which needs unprivileged user namespaces.
Docker's default seccomp profile blocks the syscalls involved (`unshare`, `mount`,
`pivot_root`, …), so out of the box Codex warns *"Codex's Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap and
needs access to create user namespaces"* and every command needs escalation.

The container therefore runs with `.devcontainer/seccomp.json`: Docker's default profile with
exactly those syscalls allowed unconditionally — nothing else is loosened. Verify from inside:

```bash
unshare -Ur true && codex sandbox -- true && echo sandbox-ok
```

`make-seccomp.sh` regenerates the file from the current upstream default profile; run it
when Docker's profile changes and commit the result. If you would rather not allow user
namespaces at all, remove the `seccomp=` line from `runArgs` and set
`sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` in `config.toml` — the container is the sandbox then.

Two things you will see that are not errors:

- `Model metadata for '<model>' not found. Defaulting to fallback metadata` at startup. Codex
  keeps a built-in table of per-model metadata (context window, reasoning support, truncation
---

Considered named volumes for `~/.claude` and `~/.codex`. Rejected: `~/.codex/config.toml` is
baked into the image, and a volume would shadow it after the first mount, silently ignoring
config changes on rebuild. Instead: `specstory sync` + a raw-transcript copy before rebuilds,
and durable context in the AGENTS files. See `.devcontainer/agent_docs/session-continuity.md`.

## 2026-09-20 — Custom seccomp profile rather than `seccomp=unconfined`

Codex's sandbox needs unprivileged user namespaces; Docker's default profile blocks them.
`unconfined` would drop the whole syscall filter. The shipped profile is upstream default +
six syscalls, regenerable by script so it can track upstream. `no-new-privileges` stays on.
Trade-off (kernel userns attack surface) is stated in README → *Security notes*.

## 2026-09-20 — Wrapper passes model/context to Codex instead of hard-coding

Codex cannot query a custom provider and `config.toml` cannot compute values. A PATH-shadowing
wrapper with `-c` overrides was the only way to keep the config in sync with the server; the
config values remain as fallbacks for when the server is down at launch.

## 2026-09-20 — Chat-template fix is a generator script, not a committed template

The template is model-specific and comes from the running server; committing one would go
stale and imply the container is Qwen-specific. The script's workflow is model-neutral; the
per-model patch table is the only model-specific part.

## 2026-09-20 — `model = "local"` kept although the server ignores it

Based on the search results, I found information about the "Decoding seccomp profile failed: invalid character '/'" error that occurs when using JetBrains dev containers with seccomp configurations.

## The Issue

The error "Decoding seccomp profile failed: invalid character '/'" occurs because seccomp only accepts "unconfined" or an inline JSON string, not a file path.

## Root Cause

When you try to pass a file path (like `/path/to/seccomp.json`) in the `runArgs` or `security_opts` configuration for dev containers, Docker's API incorrectly interprets the path as literal text rather than as a reference to load the profile from a file. This affects both relative paths (indicated by a '.' error) and absolute paths (indicated by a '/' error).

## Solution

There are a few workarounds:

1. **Use `seccomp:unconfined`**: This disables seccomp filtering but eliminates the parsing error (though this reduces security)
2. **Use an inline JSON string**: Instead of referencing a file path, embed the seccomp profile as a JSON string directly in your configuration
3. **Load the profile into the container**: Copy the seccomp profile into the container at runtime and reference it from there

This appears to be a limitation in how Docker's API handles the `runArgs` or `security_opts` parameters when dealing with file paths in dev container configurations.

## Security notes

- Secrets live in `.devcontainer/.env`, which is git-ignored. `.env.example` is the tracked template.
- Codex talks only to your own machine; no model traffic leaves the host unless you add a hosted provider.
- The Docker socket is deliberately **not** mounted; an agent in the container cannot control the host engine.
- No path to root from inside the container, so an agent that goes wrong is confined to the
  `vscode` user and the bind-mounted workspace. The remaining boundary is the container itself —
  harden that further with Docker rootless mode or userns-remap on the host.
- The hardening is enforced at two levels deliberately: the image removes the tools, and
  `no-new-privileges` blocks the whole class of escalation even if a feature or a later
  `apt-get install` puts a setuid binary back.
- The seccomp profile allows unprivileged user namespaces so Codex can sandbox its commands.
  That is the same thing a stock Linux desktop allows, and the container's own boundary is
  unchanged, but it does expose the kernel's user-namespace code to whatever runs inside.
  See *Codex's Linux sandbox* for how to turn it back off.

## Build performance

- BuildKit cache mounts hold apt's `.deb` downloads and package lists between builds.
- Layers are ordered coldest first: apt, then uv, then the pinned SpecStory and Codex downloads.
- `codex-config.toml` and `codex-wrapper.sh` are copied last, so editing them rebuilds only trivial layers, not the toolchain.
- `seccomp.json` is a run-time option, not part of the image; changing it needs a container restart, not a rebuild.

## Other architectures

MCR publishes amd64 and arm64 only. For riscv64, set the `BASE_IMAGE` build arg to `debian:trixie`;
the Dockerfile creates the `vscode` user when the base image lacks it. uv ships a `riscv64gc` build
and is installed there too. SpecStory and Codex publish no riscv64 binaries — those steps skip
themselves rather than failing the build, so you get a working container without those two tools.

35:VS Code, JetBrains and Zed pick the config up automatically when you open the folder.

**JetBrains IDEs cannot apply the profile as written.** Their Docker integration sends `runArgs`
to the engine API verbatim instead of reading the profile file the way the `docker` CLI does, so
creating the container fails with `Status 500: Decoding seccomp profile failed: invalid character
'/' looking for beginning of value` ([IJPL-67749](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IJPL-67749),

For a one-off test against a different endpoint without editing the config,
`CODEX_OSS_BASE_URL=http://host.docker.internal:9931/v1` overrides Codex's built-in OSS provider.

### Codex's Linux sandbox

Codex runs commands inside a bubblewrap sandbox, which needs unprivileged user namespaces.
Docker's default seccomp profile blocks the syscalls involved (`unshare`, `mount`,
`pivot_root`, …), so out of the box Codex warns *"Codex's Linux sandbox uses bubblewrap and
needs access to create user namespaces"* and every command needs escalation.

The container therefore runs with `.devcontainer/seccomp.json`: Docker's default profile with
exactly those syscalls allowed unconditionally — nothing else is loosened. Verify from inside:

```bash
unshare -Ur true && codex sandbox -- true && echo sandbox-ok
```

`make-seccomp.sh` regenerates the file from the current upstream default profile; run it
when Docker's profile changes and commit the result. If you would rather not allow user
namespaces at all, remove the `seccomp=` line from `runArgs` and set
`sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"` in `config.toml` — the container is the sandbox then.

**JetBrains IDEs cannot apply the profile as written.** Their Docker integration sends `runArgs`
to the engine API verbatim instead of reading the profile file the way the `docker` CLI does, so
creating the container fails with `Status 500: Decoding seccomp profile failed: invalid character
'/' looking for beginning of value` ([IJPL-67749](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IJPL-67749),
open since 2024). VS Code, the devcontainer CLI and Codespaces are fine. In JetBrains, comment out
the `seccomp=` line in `runArgs` and pick one:

- Keep the filter by making the profile the daemon's default on the host: copy `seccomp.json`
  to `/etc/docker/seccomp.json`, add `"seccomp-profile": "/etc/docker/seccomp.json"` to
  `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, and restart Docker. Every container on that host then runs with
  this profile — the stock default plus the six user-namespace syscalls.
- Or replace the value with `seccomp=unconfined`, which drops the syscall filter for this
  container entirely.

Inlining the profile's JSON into `runArgs` is not a fix: the `docker` CLI treats any value other
than `unconfined` as a file name, so that would break the other tools instead.

Two things you will see that are not errors:

_**Agent (claude-opus-5 2026-09-20 17:10:39Z)**_

The error is a JetBrains bug, not a problem with the profile — and it means Codex's sandbox is currently *not* working in your container (`unshare -Ur true` → `Operation not permitted`, `Seccomp_filters: 1` = Docker's stock profile).

**What's going on.** `runArgs` are `docker run` arguments. The `docker` CLI reads `seccomp=<file>` client-side and sends the JSON to the engine. PyCharm's dev-container support (this container is running under PyCharm 2026.2.3) talks to the engine API directly and passes the string through verbatim, so the daemon tries to JSON-decode `/home/…/seccomp.json` and chokes on the first `/`. That's JetBrains issue [IJPL-67749](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IJPL-67749), open since March 2024, same `Status 500:` prefix. VS Code, the devcontainer CLI and Codespaces are unaffected. The other two runArgs work in JetBrains (`NoNewPrivs: 1`, `host.docker.internal` resolves), so it's specifically the file-read emulation that's missing.

**Why I didn't inline the JSON instead.** The `docker` CLI treats any value other than `unconfined` as a file name, so inlining would fix JetBrains and break everything else. There's no value that works in both.

**What I changed** (nothing committed):
- `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` — restored the `seccomp=` line (it's correct per the spec) with a one-line comment pointing at the README.
- `README.md` — new paragraph under *Codex's Linux sandbox* explaining the JetBrains failure and the two workarounds; a pointer from the quick-start line that names JetBrains.
- `agent_docs/decisions.md` — dated entry for keeping the path form.

**What you need to do on your host** (I can't do or verify it from inside the container). Comment out the `seccomp=` line locally again, then either:

1. *Keeps the filter (what I'd pick):* make the profile the daemon default —
   `sudo cp .devcontainer/seccomp.json /etc/docker/seccomp.json`, add `"seccomp-profile": "/etc/docker/seccomp.json"` to `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, `sudo systemctl restart docker`. Every container on the host then gets Docker's default profile plus the six user-namespace syscalls.
2. *Simpler, weaker:* use `--security-opt=seccomp=unconfined` instead.

Then recreate the container and check: `unshare -Ur true && codex sandbox -- true && echo sandbox-ok`.

The downside of either is you carry a local, uncommitted edit to `devcontainer.json` until JetBrains fixes the bug. If you'd rather the committed file just work in PyCharm at the cost of VS Code users losing the filter, say so and I'll switch it to `unconfined` and rewrite the docs accordingly.

Sources: [IJPL-67749](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IJPL-67749/Decoding-seccomp-profile-failed), [docker/compose#2813](https://github.com/docker/compose/issues/2813) (same class of bug in older Compose)

```text
Known issue, as of 2026-09-20: JetBrains IDEs fail to create the container with `Status 500:
Decoding seccomp profile failed: invalid character '/' looking for beginning of value`. Their
dev-container support passes `runArgs` to the engine API verbatim instead of reading the profile
file the way the `docker` CLI does — [IJPL-67749](https://youtrack.jetbrains.com/issue/IJPL-67749),
open since March 2024. The devcontainer CLI (which VS Code and Codespaces use) hands `runArgs`
to `docker run` unchanged, and the `docker` CLI reads the file itself, so those should be fine —
not yet confirmed by an actual run. To stay in JetBrains until it is fixed, comment out the
`seccomp=` line in `runArgs`; everything else works, but Codex's sandbox does not — see the
previous paragraph for what to set instead.
```
